trans.sense: person who is stylish but habituated to hedonistic and immoral conduct

examples.text: We have now and then rakes in the habit of Roman senators, and grave politicians in the dress of rakes. The misfortune of the thing is, that people dress themselves in what they have a mind to be, and not what they are fit for.
examples.ref: 1711 March 26 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “THURSDAY, March 16, 1710–1711”, in The Spectator, number 14; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume I, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC, page 151:

examples.text: For honest men delight will take, / To shew you favour for his sake, / Will flatter you; and Fool and Rake / Your steps pursue: / And of your Father's name will make / A snare for you.
examples.ref: 1807, William Wordsworth, “Address to the Sons of Burns after Visiting Their Father’s Grave, Aug. 14th, 1803”, in Poems, in Two Volumes, volume II, London: […] Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], →OCLC, stanza 3, page 30:

examples.text: "He was a big old rake, full of marks and scars, and he had only an ear and a half."
examples.ref: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjø￵rnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 77:

examples.text: I have no choice but to take up the foil once again and vanquish this rake.
examples.ref: 2009, The Onion, 2:27 from the start, in Bad Boy Fencing Star Implicated In Yet Another Jewel Heist, spoken by Reggie Greengrass (Beau Baxtor):

examples.text: I am fully subscribed to the belief that reformed rakes make the very best of husbands.
